query: Which method can be used for concurrent strength–ductility improvement, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing interstitial oxygen or nitrogen into a Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi-based high-entropy alloy leads to the formation of ordered interstitial complexes that concurrently enhance both strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A base Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy produced by arc-melting without interstitial doping.
generation.intervention: Interstitial doping with oxygen or nitrogen during the alloy processing (using arc-melting and subsequent remelting procedures).
generation.conditions: Arc-melting of pure metals with the desired interstitial additives (TiO2 for oxygen doping or TiN for nitrogen doping) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere followed by repeated remelting and drop-casting into a water-cooled copper mold.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs in the oxygen-doped alloy and ONCs in the nitrogen-doped alloy).
generation.mechanism: The ordered interstitial complexes impede dislocation motion, thereby increasing yield strength, while simultaneously enhancing strain hardening which improves ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The interstitially doped HEAs (both oxygen-doped and nitrogen-doped) are expected to exhibit higher yield strength and improved ductility compared to the undoped base HEA.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) of the base Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA without interstitial doping.
generation.boundary: The extent of improvement depends on the fraction of ordered interstitial complexes formed, which in turn is influenced by the specific doping levels and processing conditions; optimal enhancement may require fine-tuning of these parameters.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports concurrent improvements, the exact quantitative differences between oxygen and nitrogen doping effects and their dependence on processing variations remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize three sets of samples: the undoped base HEA, an oxygen-doped HEA (O-2 HEA), and a nitrogen-doped HEA (N-2 HEA) using identical arc-melting and casting conditions. Conduct tensile tests and microstructural analyses on all samples.
measurements: Yield strength and elongation at fracture (ductility) via tensile testing
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM or SEM) to detect the presence and extent of ordered interstitial complexes
Internal friction or other damping measurements to support evidence of interstitial mobility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the interstitially doped HEAs do not exhibit a statistically significant concurrent increase in yield strength and ductility compared to the undoped base HEA, or if ordered interstitial complexes are not detected in the doped samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
